title: Windsurf everywhere, doing everything, all at once - Kevin Hou, Windsurf
talk_summary: Kevin Hou describes Windsurf's evolution from an IDE agent into a shared human/AI 'timeline' that ingests context from every developer surface (Slack, Docs, Figma, GitHub, MCP services) and takes actions across them (terminal, browser, PRs, review, deploy). He then argues that off-the-shelf frontier models can't handle these messy mid-workflow tasks, so they trained a smaller in-house SWE model (SWE-1) on workflow-shaped evals and a user-feedback data flywheel to reach near-frontier quality at a fraction of the cost.

takeaways.technique: Workflow-shaped evals instead of pure code-gen benchmarks
takeaways.what_they_do: They use two offline benchmarks: an end-to-end PR task benchmark (intent + starting codebase -> passing unit tests) and a 'conversational suite' benchmark that drops the model into a partially completed task/conversation and scores helpfulness, efficiency, and correctness blended.
takeaways.evidence_quote: how well the model can assist when it's being dropped into an existing user conversation or a partially completed task

takeaways.technique: Small in-house/workflow-tuned model as a cheap default
takeaways.what_they_do: They trained SWE-1 specifically on software-engineering workflows (not just code generation) and put it in the model dropdown alongside frontier models; users pick it because it matches how they work.
takeaways.evidence_quote: achieve near frontier model results at the fraction of the cost and with a significantly smaller team
takeaways.numbers: near-frontier results at a fraction of the cost

takeaways.technique: Asynchronous automated PR review with inline comments
takeaways.what_they_do: Windsurf Reviews automatically leaves comments and suggests changes asynchronously on PRs so code hitting main is production-ready, using context from prior PRs to inform description and test plan.
takeaways.evidence_quote: windsurf reviews which can automatically leave comments and suggest changes asynchronously so that you can be confident that the code that hits main is production ready

takeaways.what_they_do: They treat all developer activity (file reads, terminal history, open tabs, GitHub commits/PRs, web docs, Slack, Docs, Figma, MCP services like Notion/Linear/Stripe) as one timeline the agent reads from and writes to, rather than only editor context.

takeaways.technique: Background/parallel agents with human approval only at the end
takeaways.what_they_do: They move from synchronous human-in-loop to agents working in the background in parallel, asking the human only for final approval; they cite timelines going from 80-90% agent to a target 99% agent.
takeaways.evidence_quote: timelines are 80 to 90% agent, 10 to 20% human. But we're trying to build towards a future that gets the 99% agent and 1% human

takeaways.technique: Auto-approve safe terminal commands, gate risky ones
takeaways.what_they_do: The agent intelligently decides which terminal commands to run automatically versus which require explicit user approval.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can intelligently decide which commands we want to run automatically and which ones we want to wait and ask for explicit user approval
